title: Rust key-value store: injectable clock, key expiry, and transactions
prompt:
This repository is a small Rust crate `kv`: an in-memory key-value store (`src/store.rs`) with a Redis-like text protocol (`src/command.rs`) and integration tests in `tests/`. Run the tests with `cargo test`. Add the following, keeping the existing tests passing (`Store::new()`, `parse` and `execute` must keep working as they do) and adding tests of your own. Use no external crates.

1. New module `src/clock.rs`, re-exported from the crate root: `pub trait Clock { fn now_ms(&self) -> u64; }`; `SystemClock` (milliseconds since the Unix epoch); and `ManualClock`, a `Clone` handle whose clones share one time, with `ManualClock::new(start_ms: u64)`, `advance(&self, ms: u64)` and `set(&self, ms: u64)`.
2. Make the store generic over the clock: `Store<C: Clock = SystemClock>`. `Store::new()` keeps returning a store on the system clock; add `Store::with_clock(clock: C)`.
3. Key expiry on `Store`: `expire(&mut self, key: &str, seconds: u64) -> bool` sets the key to expire `seconds` from now and returns `false` (doing nothing) when the key does not exist. `ttl(&self, key: &str) -> i64` returns `-2` for a missing key, `-1` for a key without expiry, and otherwise the remaining time in whole seconds rounded up. A key whose expiry time has been reached (now >= expiry) behaves exactly like a missing key for `get`, `del`, `len`, `is_empty`, `ttl` and `expire`. `set` removes any expiry from the key.
4. Protocol: `EXPIRE key seconds` replies `(integer) 1` or `(integer) 0`; `TTL key` replies `(integer) <ttl>`. A `seconds` value that is not a non-negative integer is a parse error displayed as `ERR value is not an integer or out of range`. Wrong argument counts use the existing message with the lowercase command name (`expire`, `ttl`). `execute` must accept a store on any clock.
5. New module `src/session.rs`, with `Session` re-exported from the crate root: `Session<C: Clock = SystemClock>` with `Session::new(store: Store<C>)`, `store(&self) -> &Store<C>`, and `execute_line(&mut self, line: &str) -> String`, which returns the reply as text (`Response`'s display form, or `(error) <parse error>` for a line that does not parse). It supports transactions:
   - `MULTI` replies `OK` and starts queueing: each following command that parses replies `QUEUED` instead of running. A command that does not parse replies `(error) <parse error>` and marks the transaction as failed.
   - `EXEC` runs the queued commands in order and replies with one line per command, `1) <reply>`, `2) <reply>`, ..., joined with `\n`; an empty transaction replies `(empty array)`. If the transaction was marked failed, `EXEC` runs nothing and replies `(error) EXECABORT Transaction discarded because of previous errors.` Either way the transaction ends.
   - `DISCARD` drops the queue, ends the transaction, and replies `OK`.
   - `EXEC` or `DISCARD` outside a transaction reply `(error) ERR EXEC without MULTI` / `(error) ERR DISCARD without MULTI`; `MULTI` inside one replies `(error) ERR MULTI calls can not be nested` and the transaction continues.
   - `MULTI`, `EXEC` and `DISCARD` are case-insensitive like other commands.
